addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as
permanent: the branch is long-lived and lands on main
merge-only, never rebased.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.4. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

111	  - `@`-relative reads stay behind: they need a working-copy

114	- [[N]] 0.78.0-4 feat: jj-lib version gate
115	  - our side is compile-time by nature, not by compromise:
116	    the linked jj-lib is what writes ops. A `build.rs` reads
117	    the resolved version out of `Cargo.lock` and exports
118	    `JJ_LIB_VERSION` via `cargo::rustc-env`, with
119	    `rerun-if-changed` on the lock.
120	  - read `$CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/Cargo.lock` directly rather
121	    than walking ancestors: we are not a workspace, and a
122	    walk can bind a sibling project's lock, which is worse
123	    than failing
124	  - their side is `jj -V`, printing `jj 0.43.0-<hash>`, so
125	    compare the triple by prefix match or regex, never whole
126	    string equality
127	  - a version stamp in the repo data would beat asking the
128	    binary, but the one that exists is the wrong one: the
129	    index carries a format version, and it is self-healing
130	    derived data whose constant is `pub(super)`, while the
131	    op store, the thing we would be co-writing, carries none
132	  - rests on jj-cli and jj-lib releasing in lockstep; verify
133	    against the jj-cli manifest and record the assumption,
134	    since equality becomes the wrong test if they diverge
135	  - refuse on the write path only, with an explicit override
136	    flag, so a jj upgrade never blocks a read
137	  - the `.vc-config.toml` pin turns a `$PATH` sample into a
138	    declaration, but only matters once more than one jj is in
139	    play; it stays a Todo
140	- [[N]] 0.78.0-5 refactor: jj-lib mutations
141	  - commit, describe, bookmark set/track, fetch, push, plus
142	    the `@`-relative reads deferred from `-3`
143	- [[N]] 0.78.0-6 fix: jj-lib index-lock retry
144	  - bugs.md #1, with the `git init --bare` to gix rider
145	  - the retry classifies by error variant rather than
146	    substring, which is the real win: `SpawnInPath` and
147	    `UnsupportedGitOption` are never retryable, and treating
148	    the whole `Subprocess` arm as retryable would loop
149	    forever on a missing git binary
150	- [[N]] 0.78.0 refactor: jj-lib migration (close-out)
151	
152	##### Decisions at cycle open
153	
154	- **All three pieces**, decided 2026-07-30: jj-lib for reads,
155	  jj-lib for mutations, and the index-lock retry that is the
156	  headline prize. The 2026-07-29 session ended undecided
157	  between this and deferring mutations.
158	- **What changed is the coexistence objection, not the
159	  evidence.** The risk section concluded the coupling was
160	  "unenforceable, probably fine" because a `jj --version`
161	  check cannot answer whether two versions are compatible.
162	  That evaluates it as a compatibility oracle. As a guard on
163	  our own writes it fits the actual risk direction: the
164	  dangerous case is an old jj reading an op written by a
165	  newer jj-lib, and refusing to write on a mismatch closes
166	  exactly that. The safe direction, a newer jj reading our
167	  older op, is something jj must support anyway, since the
168	  user's own older jj wrote into that repo first.
169	- **The gate lands at `-4`, before the mutations at `-5`**, so
170	  mutations arrive in a repo that already refuses on
171	  mismatch. The cost is one commit whose check guards nothing
172	  yet, which reads oddly in isolation; folding it into `-5`
173	  would avoid that but make one rung do two things.
174	- **Deferring mutations was not free**, which is what settled
175	  it. The trapezoid reshape at 0.79.0 is a `jj rebase`, so
176	  "reads only" would leave that cycle either spawning or
177	  waiting.
178	
179	##### The 0.43 bump was a preview of the cost

  - `jj log` templates become `Commit` accessors
  - `@`-relative reads stay behind: they need a working-copy
    snapshot, which is an op-store write, so they move with
    the mutations
- [[N]] 0.78.0-4 feat: jj-lib version gate
  - our side is compile-time by nature, not by compromise:
    the linked jj-lib is what writes ops. A `build.rs` reads
    the resolved version out of `Cargo.lock` and exports
    `JJ_LIB_VERSION` via `cargo::rustc-env`, with
    `rerun-if-changed` on the lock.
  - read `$CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/Cargo.lock` directly rather
    than walking ancestors: we are not a workspace, and a
    walk can bind a sibling project's lock, which is worse
    than failing
  - their side is `jj -V`, printing `jj 0.43.0-<hash>`, so
    compare the triple by prefix match or regex, never whole
    string equality
  - a version stamp in the repo data would beat asking the
    binary, but the one that exists is the wrong one: the
    index carries a format version, and it is self-healing
    derived data whose constant is `pub(super)`, while the
    op store, the thing we would be co-writing, carries none
  - rests on jj-cli and jj-lib releasing in lockstep; verify
    against the jj-cli manifest and record the assumption,
    since equality becomes the wrong test if they diverge
  - refuse on the write path only, with an explicit override
    flag, so a jj upgrade never blocks a read
  - the `.vc-config.toml` pin turns a `$PATH` sample into a
    declaration, but only matters once more than one jj is in
    play; it stays a Todo
- [[N]] 0.78.0-5 refactor: jj-lib mutations
  - commit, describe, bookmark set/track, fetch, push, plus
    the `@`-relative reads deferred from `-3`
- [[N]] 0.78.0-6 fix: jj-lib index-lock retry
  - bugs.md #1, with the `git init --bare` to gix rider
  - the retry classifies by error variant rather than
    substring, which is the real win: `SpawnInPath` and
    `UnsupportedGitOption` are never retryable, and treating
    the whole `Subprocess` arm as retryable would loop
    forever on a missing git binary
- [[N]] 0.78.0 refactor: jj-lib migration (close-out)

##### Decisions at cycle open

- **All three pieces**, decided 2026-07-30: jj-lib for reads,
  jj-lib for mutations, and the index-lock retry that is the
  headline prize. The 2026-07-29 session ended undecided
  between this and deferring mutations.
- **What changed is the coexistence objection, not the
  evidence.** The risk section concluded the coupling was
  "unenforceable, probably fine" because a `jj --version`
  check cannot answer whether two versions are compatible.
  That evaluates it as a compatibility oracle. As a guard on
  our own writes it fits the actual risk direction: the
  dangerous case is an old jj reading an op written by a
  newer jj-lib, and refusing to write on a mismatch closes
  exactly that. The safe direction, a newer jj reading our
  older op, is something jj must support anyway, since the
  user's own older jj wrote into that repo first.
- **The gate lands at `-4`, before the mutations at `-5`**, so
  mutations arrive in a repo that already refuses on
  mismatch. The cost is one commit whose check guards nothing
  yet, which reads oddly in isolation; folding it into `-5`
  would avoid that but make one rung do two things.
- **Deferring mutations was not free**, which is what settled
  it. The trapezoid reshape at 0.79.0 is a `jj rebase`, so
  "reads only" would leave that cycle either spawning or
  waiting.

583	## Design risk: op-store coexistence
584	
585	In-process op-store writes must coexist with the user's
586	external `jj` CLI driving the same repos. Investigated
587	2026-07-29 (jj-lib 0.41 source, installed jj 0.40.0, jj's
588	published docs). Findings, and why the obvious mitigation
589	does not work:
590	
591	- **Today there is no risk at all.** vc-x1 spawns the user's
592	  `jj` for every mutation, so it inherits their version. The
593	  migration *introduces* the coupling; it does not inherit
594	  one.
595	- **Structural change fails closed.** `repo.rs:491-569` /
596	  `workspace.rs:513` raise `StoreLoadError::UnsupportedType`
597	  when a `type` file names a backend the library lacks, so a
598	  future `op_store/type` we don't know is a hard error, not a
599	  guess.
600	- **The index self-heals.** It carries an explicit format
601	  version (`COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION = 6`,
602	  checked at `default_index/readonly.rs:303`), and
603	  `default_index/store.rs:560` responds to a mismatch by
604	  reindexing, not erroring. Derived data; costs time only.
605	  Reading those bytes ourselves is inert (it does not
606	  trigger the rebuild), but the constant is `pub(super)`, so
607	  a check of our own would duplicate a private constant and
608	  an internal file layout.
609	- **The op store has no version stamp.** It serializes with
610	  protobuf (`simple_op_store.rs:159-218`), whose evolution
611	  rule is that unknown fields are skipped. So an evolutionary
612	  change (same backend type, new fields) is *undetectable*
613	  by construction: a reader cannot distinguish "field absent"
614	  from "field present and unknown to me". The realistic
615	  failure is silent information loss, not corruption.
616	- **jj publishes no compatibility policy.** Checked the core
617	  tenets, architecture, and concurrency pages: no stability
618	  guarantee for on-disk formats, and only a bare footnote
619	  mentioning "automatic upgrades of the repo format" with no
620	  detail. Everything above is behavior read out of one
621	  version's source, which they are free to change.

## Design risk: op-store coexistence

In-process op-store writes must coexist with the user's
external `jj` CLI driving the same repos. Investigated
2026-07-29 (jj-lib 0.41 source, installed jj 0.40.0, jj's
published docs). Findings, and why the obvious mitigation
does not work:

- **Today there is no risk at all.** vc-x1 spawns the user's
  `jj` for every mutation, so it inherits their version. The
  migration *introduces* the coupling; it does not inherit
  one.
- **Structural change fails closed.** `repo.rs:491-569` /
  `workspace.rs:513` raise `StoreLoadError::UnsupportedType`
  when a `type` file names a backend the library lacks, so a
  future `op_store/type` we don't know is a hard error, not a
  guess.
- **The index self-heals.** It carries an explicit format
  version (`COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION = 6`,
  checked at `default_index/readonly.rs:303`), and
  `default_index/store.rs:560` responds to a mismatch by
  reindexing, not erroring. Derived data; costs time only.
  Reading those bytes ourselves is inert (it does not
  trigger the rebuild), but the constant is `pub(super)`, so
  a check of our own would duplicate a private constant and
  an internal file layout.
- **The op store has no version stamp.** It serializes with
  protobuf (`simple_op_store.rs:159-218`), whose evolution
  rule is that unknown fields are skipped. So an evolutionary
  change (same backend type, new fields) is *undetectable*
  by construction: a reader cannot distinguish "field absent"
  from "field present and unknown to me". The realistic
  failure is silent information loss, not corruption.
- **jj publishes no compatibility policy.** Checked the core
  tenets, architecture, and concurrency pages: no stability
  guarantee for on-disk formats, and only a bare footnote
  mentioning "automatic upgrades of the repo format" with no
  detail. Everything above is behavior read out of one
  version's source, which they are free to change.
- **Concurrent writers are by design**, which helps the other
  half of the question: "To avoid depending on lock files,
  Jujutsu takes a different approach by accepting that
  concurrent changes can always happen" (concurrency page).
  Operations are content-addressed and op heads are tracked
  by filename.
- **A `jj --version` check does not work.** Users can have
  several jj binaries installed (this workspace has both
  `vc-x1` and `vc-x1-dev`); what our `$PATH` resolves to says
  nothing about what an editor integration, another shell, or
  a later session will run against the same repo. The check
  is a sample, not a gate.

We think the residual risk is therefore low-probability,
silent, and low-blast-radius, but it cannot be enforced
away, so taking it on should be a decision rather than a
step the ladder assumes.

# References

[1]: /notes/bugs.md
[2]: /notes/chores/chores-12.md#docs-pordual-parity-design-0610
[3]: /notes/chores/chores-03.md#submodule--ochid-circular-dependency-bug-0290
[4]: /notes/chores/chores-06.md#non-tracking-remote-bookmark-detection-design
[5]: /notes/design-cli/por-dual-parity.md

content.text:
Settled at cycle open (2026-07-30), written down in the ladder but not yet built; rung `-2` is the docs commit that records it and `-4` implements it. Three sources, three different roles:

**1. Our version: compile time, out of `Cargo.lock`.** The linked jj-lib is what writes ops, so our side is compile-time by nature, not by compromise. `build.rs` reads the resolved jj-lib version from the lock and exports `JJ_LIB_VERSION` via `cargo::rustc-env`, with `rerun-if-changed` on the lock. It reads `$CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/Cargo.lock` directly rather than walking ancestors: we are not a workspace, and a walk can bind a sibling project's lock, which is worse than failing.

**2. Their version: `jj -V` at runtime.** Output is `jj 0.43.0-<hash>`, so compare the triple by prefix match or regex, never whole-string equality. This rests on jj-cli and jj-lib releasing in lockstep; verify against the jj-cli manifest and record the assumption, since equality becomes the wrong test if they ever diverge.

**3. The version in the repo data: not used.** A stamp in the data would beat asking a binary, but the one that exists is the wrong one. The index carries a format version (`notes/refactor-20260716.md:600`) and it is self-healing derived data whose constant is `pub(super)`, so checking it means duplicating a private constant and an internal file layout. The op store, the thing we would actually be co-writing, carries no stamp at all: protobuf with unknown fields skipped, so an evolutionary change is undetectable by construction.

**Enforcement.** Refuse on the write path only, with an explicit override flag, so a jj upgrade never blocks a read. The `.vc-config.toml` pin turns a `$PATH` sample into a declaration but only matters once more than one jj is in play; it stays a Todo.

**What the check claims, and what it doesn't.** The old objection at `notes/refactor-20260716.md:628` still holds on its own terms: `$PATH` is a sample, not a gate, since an editor integration or another shell can run a different jj against the same repo. What changed is what we ask of the check. As a compatibility oracle it fails; as a guard on our own writes it fits the risk direction, because the dangerous case is an old jj reading an op written by newer jj-lib, and refusing to write on mismatch closes exactly that. The safe direction, a newer jj reading our older op, is something jj must support anyway, since the user's own older jj wrote into that repo first.

The plain version: we trust our compiled-in jj-lib version as fact, ask the user's `jj` binary its version and compare the numbers loosely, and ignore what is on disk because jj does not record anything useful there. On a mismatch we refuse to write, never to read, and there is a flag to override.

48	/// Banner string emitted as the first line of normal command runs
49	/// and shown at the top of subcommand `--help` output. Built from
50	/// `Cargo.toml`'s name + version at compile time so it stays in
51	/// sync with the bumped version.
52	const BANNER: &str = concat!(env!("CARGO_PKG_NAME"), " ", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"));
53	
54	/// Top-level about line — name, version, and the project tagline
55	/// on a single line. Used as the top-level `about` so `vc-x1 -h`
56	/// reads as one banner-plus-tagline header instead of two stacked
57	/// lines.
58	const TOP_ABOUT: &str = concat!(
59	    env!("CARGO_PKG_NAME"),
60	    " ",
61	    env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"),
62	    " - jj workspace tooling"
63	);
64	
65	/// Build the clap command tree with `BANNER` set as `before_help`
66	/// on every subcommand (transitively). Top-level skips `before_help`
67	/// because its own `about` already carries the name+version+tagline.
68	/// Walks via `mut_subcommand` so individual subcommand
69	/// `#[command(long_about = ...)]` blocks don't have to repeat the
70	/// banner text.
71	fn cli_with_banner() -> clap::Command {
72	    fn add_to_subs(mut cmd: clap::Command) -> clap::Command {
73	        let names: Vec<String> = cmd
74	            .get_subcommands()
75	            .map(|c| c.get_name().to_string())
76	            .collect();
77	        for name in names {
78	            cmd = cmd.mut_subcommand(name, add_with_banner);
79	        }
80	        cmd
81	    }
82	    fn add_with_banner(mut cmd: clap::Command) -> clap::Command {
83	        cmd = cmd.before_help(BANNER);
84	        let names: Vec<String> = cmd
85	            .get_subcommands()
86	            .map(|c| c.get_name().to_string())
87	            .collect();
88	        for name in names {
89	            cmd = cmd.mut_subcommand(name, add_with_banner);
90	        }
91	        cmd
92	    }
93	    add_to_subs(Cli::command())
94	}

97	#[command(about = TOP_ABOUT, max_term_width = 80)]
98	pub struct Cli {
99	    /// Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then
100	    /// continue. With no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
101	    ///
102	    /// Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after
103	    /// printing): the banner now rides along with normal
104	    /// subcommand execution rather than gating it, so scripts
105	    /// can capture the version *and* the command's output in

1	# Code conventions
2	
3	Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
4	wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).
5	
6	Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
7	[custom.md](../custom.md).
8	
9	## Line width
10	
11	Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
12	default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
13	applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).
14	
15	## Doc comments on every file, function, and method
16	
17	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
18	a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
19	is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
20	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
21	
22	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
23	inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
24	explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
25	non-obvious WHY.
26	
27	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
28	by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
29	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
30	help.
31	
32	## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
33	
34	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
35	`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
36	patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
37	lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
38	in scope:
39	
40	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
41	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
42	  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.
43	
44	When one is used, three obligations attach:
45	
46	- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
47	  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
48	    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
49	  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
50	    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
51	  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
52	    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
53	- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
54	  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
55	- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
56	  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:
57	
58	  ```toml
59	  [lints.clippy]
60	  unwrap_used = "warn"
61	  expect_used = "warn"
62	  ```
63	
64	  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
65	  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by
66	  the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The vc-x1-work-repo-template's
67	  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)
68	
69	```rust
70	let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
71	let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious
72	
73	match matches.len() {
74	    1 => {
75	        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
76	        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
77	        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
78	    }
79	    // ...
80	}
81	```
82	
83	Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
84	behavior.

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by
  the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The vc-x1-work-repo-template's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## File reads: read the slice you need
12	
13	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs; grep or read
14	further on demand.
15	
16	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
17	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
18	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read further only when chasing a
19	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
20	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
21	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it first.
22	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
23	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
24	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
25	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
26	  need.
27	
28	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
29	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
30	to historical files.
31	
32	## Notes references
33	
34	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
35	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
36	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
37	single-bracketed.
38	
39	## Reference numbering
40	
41	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
42	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
43	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
44	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
45	
46	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
47	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
48	file's number; to cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
49	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
50	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
51	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no definition here. To
52	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
53	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
54	
55	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
56	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
57	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a section's `Commits:` line.
58	See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the exact shape.
59	
60	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
61	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
62	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
63	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
64	definitions move; every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
65	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
66	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
67	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
68	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
69	slots out of document order).
70	
71	## Markdown anchor links
72	
73	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
74	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
75	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
76	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
77	official spec for auto-generated anchors; the de-facto reference implementation is
78	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
79	
80	## Todo format
81	
82	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
83	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
84	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
85	description with reference links to more detail.
86	
87	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
88	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
89	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
90	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
91	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
92	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
93	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
94	
95	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
96	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
97	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
98	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
99	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
100	
101	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
102	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
103	
104	Example shape:
105	
106	```
107	# Todo
108	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
109	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
110	
111	# Done
112	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
113	
114	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
115	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
116	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
117	```
118	
119	## Retiring Done entries
120	
121	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
122	log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:
123	
124	- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
125	  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
126	- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
127	  version-of-record.
128	
129	Migration mechanics:
130	
131	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
132	  number).
133	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
134	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
135	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
136	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
137	
138	## Chores conventions
139	
140	### Headings and entries that record a commit
141	
142	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
143	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
144	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
145	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
146	`(<version>)` suffix**; see
147	[Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
148	header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
149	`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
150	title.
151	
152	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
153	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
154	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
155	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
156	
157	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
158	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
159	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
160	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
161	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
162	
163	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
164	free-form text; the convention applies going forward.
165	
166	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
167	
168	A chores section is: a `Commits:` line (first line under the header; see below), then
169	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
170	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
171	per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
172	"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
173	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
174	restates the other.
175	
176	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own `### As-built ladder`
177	rung + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
178	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
179	cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
180	the pointer, so the two don't drift.
181	
182	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
183	promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
184	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
185	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
186	direction).
187	
188	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
189	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
190	narrative; `Commits:` links them.
191	
192	### Chores commit references
193	
194	The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:` line citing the git commit(s)
195	that section records:
196	
197	```
198	## refactor: extract config loader
199	
200	Commits: [[3]]
201	
202	<intro paragraph...>
203	```
204	
205	`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
206	[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render:
207	`Commits: [[3]]`, or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the
208	`[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and
209	CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition puts the **commit
210	URL** as the destination, with the **full 40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
211	
212	```
213	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
214	```
215	
216	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
217	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
218	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
219	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
220	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
221	
222	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
223	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
224	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every section opens with an
225	**empty `Commits:`**, and each push backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push
226	made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is
227	the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
228	[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
`(<version>)` suffix**; see
[Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
title.

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text; the convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: a `Commits:` line (first line under the header; see below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
restates the other.

The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own `### As-built ladder`
rung + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
the pointer, so the two don't drift.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; `Commits:` links them.

### Chores commit references

The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:` line citing the git commit(s)
that section records:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

Commits: [[3]]

<intro paragraph...>
```

`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render:
`Commits: [[3]]`, or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the
`[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and
CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition puts the **commit
URL** as the destination, with the **full 40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every section opens with an
**empty `Commits:`**, and each push backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push
made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is
the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

content.text:
Done, uncommitted in the working copy. `--version` now answers all three questions:

```
vc-x1-dev 0.78.0-1
jj-lib 0.43.0
jj-data work commit=git op=simple_op_store op-heads=simple_op_heads_store index=default submodule=default working-copy=local
jj-data bot  commit=git op=simple_op_store op-heads=simple_op_heads_store index=default submodule=default working-copy=local
jj-data note: backend type names only; jj-lib exposes no on-disk format version
```

**What the data actually yields.** Reading through jj-lib's public API only, the answer is six backend *type* names and no number anywhere. `RepoLoader::init_from_file_system` is documented as reading "the various `.jj/repo/<backend>/type` files", and its accessors (`store().backend().name()`, `op_store()`, `op_heads_store()`, `index_store()`, `submodule_store()`, plus `working_copy()`) hand back exactly those strings. jj-lib 0.43 has zero `pub fn *version*` and zero public `*_VERSION` constant. The commit index's `COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION = 6` is `pub(super)`; the only public surface carrying it is `ReadonlyIndexLoadError::UnexpectedVersion`, which you can reach only by *failing* a load, and `DefaultIndexStore` swallows that and reindexes. So the risk section's "the op store has no version stamp" is now observed, not inferred.

**Files.** `build.rs` (new) resolves jj-lib's version from `Cargo.lock` and exports `JJ_LIB_VERSION`; `src/version.rs` (new) holds the report; `src/main.rs` calls it. Two judgment calls worth your eye:

- The build script is `-4`'s mechanism arriving early. jj-lib gives no runtime way to ask its own version, so printing it at all requires it. `-4` then adds only the `jj -V` comparison and the write-path refusal. Relevant evidence for that gate: installed `jj -V` prints `jj 0.43.0-89f62ede8c1c611eaf134c0c49252efd65c7945d`, matching the linked jj-lib 0.43.0, so the lockstep assumption holds today.
- The full report prints only for a bare `-V`. As a rider on a subcommand, `-V` stays one banner line, so it loads no workspace and scripts capturing it see what they saw before.

`data_version` deliberately stops at `Workspace::load` and never calls `load_at_head`, since resolving op heads can merge divergent ones, which is a write.

I dropped the unit tests I first wrote in `build.rs`: `cargo test` never compiles a build script as a test target, so they would have been the exact "looks like a guarantee, isn't" shape your Todo #2 is about. The parser is covered instead by a real test asserting the compiled-in version matches `Cargo.lock`, scanned a different way so a drifted parser cannot agree with itself. No `unwrap`/`expect` in non-test code; the one `.expect` is in that test.

**Validation.** `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test` (514 passing), and `cargo install --path . --locked` all clean, each run separately. `validate-todo` clean.

**TODO.md** rung `-2` now carries the measured output and the mechanism, plus one open item flagged for you: a rung that ships code does not obviously keep a `docs:` title.

The plain version: `vc-x1-dev --version` now prints our version, the jj library version we compile against, and what each repo's jj data says about itself. That last one turns out to be just the names of the storage backends, never a version number, which confirms what we had only reasoned about. Nothing is committed, and the title question is yours to settle.

content.text:
Short answer: no. Protobuf's wire format is the reason the coupling is undetectable, not a way out of it.

**What is actually on disk.** A proto3 message serializes to a sequence of (field number, wire type) keys plus payload bytes. No message name, no schema identifier, no version, no field names. That is the whole design: a reader that meets tag 47 and doesn't know it can compute the payload length from the wire type and skip it. The skippability *is* the absence of type information. The schema exists only in `simple_op_store.proto`, compiled into each side separately.

**What you could recover, and why it isn't a gate.** From a blob you can enumerate which tags are present and their wire types. That is a sample of what one writer populated, not a schema, and it fails as a check three ways:

- An absent optional field is indistinguishable from a field the writer never heard of. Proto3 has no presence for scalars, so "not set" and "not known" are the same bytes.
- New tags appear only once a newer jj actually populates them. A newer jj that has the field but hasn't used it looks byte-identical to an older one.
- jj-lib won't show you the unknown tags anyway. prost's derived `merge_field` routes an unrecognized tag to `encoding::skip_field`, which advances past it and discards it. There is no `unknown_fields` set to inspect. Recovering them means decoding the wire format ourselves, which is outside jj-lib by definition.

**Why "save our versions at compile time and compare" only has one operand.** `jj_lib::protos` is `pub`, so our schema is reachable at compile time. But equality needs two values, and the other side publishes nothing: the data carries no stamp, and jj the binary carries no schema id. A stamp we write ourselves records only what *we* last wrote; jj never updates it, so a jj write leaves it stale and silently wrong. It also points the wrong way for the risk that matters, since the endangered reader is the user's older jj, which will never look at a file we invented. That is why `jj -V` stays the second operand: not because a version is the right thing to compare, but because it is the only thing the other side emits. It is a proxy for schema identity, and we should say so in the policy rather than implying it is the thing itself.

**One finding here does change something.** The risk section says the realistic failure is "silent information loss". prost's skip-and-discard lets us name the mechanism instead of gesturing at it: our jj-lib decodes a View written by a newer jj, drops the fields it doesn't know, converts what's left into the domain `View`, and the next transaction writes a fresh View built from that lossy struct. Content addressing means the original blob survives under its own id, so this is loss of current state, not destruction of history, and an older operation could in principle be recovered from. Still, it is concrete and it makes the `-4` gate look better justified than "unenforceable, probably fine" did.

**Where the compile-time idea does pay, in a different job.** Not as a gate against jj, but as a bump detector on our own side: fingerprint the op-store schema at build time and fail loudly when a jj-lib bump changes it. That would turn "a green build after a bump is not evidence" into a red build for exactly the op-store-shape class. Two honest costs: it catches nothing semantic, so the 0.43 glob-versus-substring change would still slip through; and Rust gives no reflection, so the fingerprint has to come from hashing jj-lib's shipped `.proto` files, which a build script cannot locate cleanly (cargo hands us only our own `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, and there is no env var pointing at a dependency's source). A test that resolves the path via `cargo metadata` or the `CARGO_HOME` registry layout would work, at the price of a test that knows about cargo's directory layout. The cheap alternative is a checklist line: diff `simple_op_store.proto` on every jj-lib bump.

The plain version: the data cannot tell us what schema wrote it, by design, so there is nothing to compare our compile-time version against. content.text:
Agreed, and the write premise makes the rule better-founded than the notes currently argue.

**It corrects the recorded rationale.** The decision text in `TODO.md` says the safe direction is "a newer jj reading our older op, something jj must support anyway". That holds for jj *reading*. It stops holding once you put our writes in the picture, because the loss is symmetric:

- ours newer than theirs: we write fields their jj skips, and their next write drops them.
- ours older than theirs: they wrote fields we skip, and our next write drops them.

Same mechanism both ways, prost discarding unknown tags and the next writer serializing from the lossy struct. So there is no safe direction to exempt, and `!=` is the right test rather than an ordering comparison. That is a stronger argument than the one recorded, and `-2` should carry it, since the current text would justify a one-sided gate.

**It also settles why equality, not compatibility.** We cannot compute compatibility: the data publishes no schema and jj publishes no policy. An unequal pair is not "incompatible", it is "unknown", and the only correct response to unknown on a write path is stop. Strict equality is the conservative reading of an unanswerable question, which is the right way to lose the argument.

**Sharp edges worth pinning down before `-4` builds it.**

*What A and B literally are.* A is our linked jj-lib from `Cargo.lock`, `0.43.0`. B is the triple parsed out of `jj -V`, which prints `jj 0.43.0-89f62ede8c1c611eaf134c0c49252efd65c7945d`. Comparing triples means a jj built from git between releases claims `0.43.0` while being arbitrarily far ahead of the release we link. The hash suffix is the only thing that could distinguish them and we cannot map a hash to a schema, so that hole stays open. Worth writing down as a known limit rather than discovering it later.

*What the rule actually guarantees.* Not "no old jj will misread our op". Only "we never write with a jj-lib differing from the jj we can see". The `$PATH` sample objection from the risk section survives intact: an editor integration running a different jj is outside the gate. The gate is honest about its own scope or it becomes the same looks-like-a-guarantee defect the cycle is deleting.

*Where it fires.* Preflight, before the first write of an invocation, not at the mutation itself. Stopping halfway through a push leaves worse state than never starting. That argues the check belongs at the facade's write entry, evaluated once per process and cached, not per operation. Ironic but unavoidable: the check is a `jj` spawn in the cycle that ends spawning, though one per invocation on their side of the boundary.

*What stop says.* The message has to name both operands and all three exits: upgrade jj, re-pin jj-lib and rebuild, or pass the override. An override that is a per-invocation flag rather than a config key, because a config key gets set once during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

**The cost you are accepting.** Every jj release stops vc-x1 writes until the lock is bumped and revalidated. That is the treadmill, now with teeth. The bump-detector idea from before is what would eventually let an override be *safe* rather than merely available, since an unchanged op-store schema hash would mean the version inequality is cosmetic. Not now, but it is the reason to keep that idea alive.

The plain version: yes, stop on any mismatch, and for a better reason than we wrote down. Because we write too, an old jj and a new jj can each destroy what the other wrote, so neither side is the safe side and there is no version ordering worth reasoning about. The rule should be blunt, fire before anything is written, and be honest that it only checks the jj it can see.

content.text:
Your instinct is not just caution, it is already true in this codebase. Three read paths write, and we have all three in hand:

- `load_at_head()` resolves op heads, and when there are several divergent ones it merges them and writes a new operation. Our `--version` code deliberately stops at `Workspace::load` for exactly this reason.
- The index self-heals. A stale or format-mismatched index makes `DefaultIndexStore` reindex and write new segment files. `COMMIT_INDEX_SEGMENT_FILE_FORMAT_VERSION` is a compile-time constant in jj-lib, so a mismatched pair does not just risk this, it guarantees churn: we write segments at our version, their jj rewrites them at theirs, back and forth.
- Any `@`-relative read needs a working-copy snapshot, which writes `tree_state` and can create a commit. That is already why `-3` defers those reads to `-5`.

So "read" in jj-lib does not mean "does not write", it means "does not write anything the caller asked for". A gate scoped to writes would be scoped to a distinction the library does not actually honor.

**This retires a bullet in the recorded design.** `-4` currently says "refuse on the write path only, with an explicit override flag, so a jj upgrade never blocks a read". That is now the wrong shape for the same reason `-2` is revising the risk section, and it should be superseded in the same breath rather than left to be discovered mid-implementation.

**One carve-out, and I do not think it costs you anything.** A command that never opens a repo cannot write to one. That set is small and nameable: `--version`, `--help`, shell completion, and the pure-markdown commands (`fix-todo`, `validate-todo`). Gating those buys no safety and costs real things: a `jj -V` spawn on every tab press for completion, and a hard `jj`-on-`$PATH` dependency for `validate-todo TODO.md`, which is a markdown linter. It also makes the diagnostic self-defeating, since `--version` is the command whose whole job is to show you the mismatch, and it would refuse to run.

The clean resolution for `--version` specifically: gate before it gathers the `jj-data` lines. On a mismatch it prints the two versions and the verdict, and says the repo lines are withheld. It still answers the question you ran it to ask, without touching the repo.

The carve-out is worth defining as "provably does not open a repo" rather than as a list, because that is a property you can test rather than a promise you maintain by hand.

**Precise ordering.** Literally-first is not implementable: before clap parses you do not know whether this is a completion request, and you have no `-v`/`--log` set up to report the failure through. The ordering you want is parse, init logging, gate, then everything else, with nothing between the gate and the first repo access. That is "first" in the sense that matters, and it is a stronger statement than the write-path version because it holds regardless of which paths turn out to write.

**Costs to accept, stated plainly.** One `jj -V` spawn per invocation. A jj upgrade stops vc-x1 entirely, not just its writes, until the lock is bumped and revalidated, so the override flag stops being a nicety and becomes the thing that keeps the tool usable on the day jj releases. And `jj` missing from `$PATH` becomes a hard failure for everything outside the carve-out, which is defensible but should be a distinct message from a version mismatch, since the fix is different.

**What "until we test it" could concretely mean.** Hash every file under `.jj/` (both repos), run one command, hash again, diff. Run that per command against a deliberately mismatched jj-lib. The index case will light up immediately, which is itself the evidence for keeping the gate broad; anything that comes back genuinely inert is a candidate for relaxing later, backed by a measurement instead of an assumption. That is the path from pedantic to calibrated, and it is cheap enough to build when you want it.

The plain version: you are right, and we can prove it rather than assume it, since we already know three read paths that write. Gate at startup, stop on any mismatch, with the only exception being commands that never open a repo at all, because those cannot hurt anything and gating them would break a markdown linter and the very command you would use to diagnose the mismatch. This does mean a jj upgrade stops the tool until we rebuild, so the override flag matters more than it did.

Yes, it fits, with one problem and one structural doubt worth settling before anything is written.

**The title no longer covers the rung.** `-2` has already grown a `build.rs`, a new module, and a CLI behavior change. That is not a `docs:` commit, and hard rule 9 ties the commit title to the chores header and the ladder rung, so a title that misdescribes the commit misdescribes all three. Two honest ways out, and I prefer the second:

- One rung, retitled to something compound like `feat: version reporting + coupling policy`. Cheap, but it is the same "one rung doing two things" you rejected when you decided the gate lands at `-4` rather than folded into `-5`.
- Split. `-2 feat: report jj-lib and jj-data versions` (the code, already sitting in the working copy) and `-3 docs: jj-lib version coupling policy` (the prose). The order is right: the policy is written from measured output, so the measurement commits first. The cost is renumbering `-3` through `-6` up to `-4` through `-7`, which touches four ladder bullets and their detail anchors.

The split also gives the docs rung a real job. `0.75.1`, `0.76.1`, `0.77.2` and `0.77.3` were all prose-only commits, so it is a shape this ladder already uses.

**The structural doubt: chores is the wrong home for a standing policy.** Your plan sends this text to `chores-15.md` at close-out. Chores is append-mostly history, organized by when work happened. But the write gate is not history, it governs what the tool does from `-4` onward, and someone asking "why does vc-x1 refuse to run" in six months should not have to know which cycle produced the answer. The one-home rule is about not duplicating text, not about everything living in the same file, so I would split by *kind*, not by convenience:

- The policy proper goes in `notes/`, next to the `## Design risk: op-store coexistence` section it supersedes, since it is that section's replacement rather than a commentary on it. Whether that is inside `refactor-20260716.md` or its own file turns on whether the policy outlives the refactor program, and it does, because the gate ships in the product.
- The cycle narrative goes in `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and moves to chores verbatim: what we decided, when, from what evidence, and which recorded conclusions it retired.

They cross-link, neither restates. That is the same division `notes.md` already draws between the commit body and the chores section.

**Sections I would create in TODO.md**, as `#####` under the stage heading, matching the existing `##### 0.78.0-0` pattern so the ladder bullets can link to them:

- `##### 0.78.0-2 feat: report jj-lib and jj-data versions`: the three sources and why each is what it is; the bare-`-V`-only decision and its script-compatibility reason; `build.rs` arriving two rungs early because jj-lib publishes no version at runtime; and the build-script tests I deleted, since "cargo test never compiles a build script" is exactly the kind of thing that gets rediscovered.
- `##### 0.78.0-3 docs: jj-lib version coupling policy`: the rung's own record.
- `##### What the data records about itself`: the measured backend-type line, and the protobuf finding that there is no type information on the wire at all, with the three reasons tag-sniffing cannot substitute. This is the section that turns the risk section's inference into observation.
- `##### Why equality, and why at startup`: the two findings that retire recorded rationale. Symmetric loss, because prost discards unknown tags and the next writer serializes from the lossy struct, so there is no safe direction to exempt. And reads that write, with the three concrete paths, so the gate cannot be scoped to writes.

**Two wrinkles in "verbatim".** The heading markers cannot survive the move: a `#####` under this stage's `####` becomes `###` under the chores `##`. The prose is verbatim, the levels shift. And the `##### <version> <title>` headers have to be final before the push, since hard rule 9 makes them equal to the commit titles, which is another reason to settle the split now rather than after the code commits.

**Outside TODO.md, three edits ride with the docs rung**: the risk section's `jj --version` conclusion, `-4`'s "refuse on the write path only" bullet, and the "Decisions at cycle open" claim that a newer jj reading our older op is the safe direction. All three are superseded by the same two findings, so they should move together or the file will argue with itself.

One piece of bookkeeping: the push that opens `-2` is also the one that backfills `-1`'s `[[N]]` to `[[22]]`.

The plain version: the discussion belongs here, but the rung as titled no longer matches what it contains, so I would split it into a code rung and a docs rung and renumber the rest. And I would not send the policy itself to chores, because chores is a dated history file and this policy governs future behavior; the narrative goes to chores, the rule goes in `notes/` beside the risk analysis it replaces.
